chapters.title: Start a project
chapters.subtitle: From an empty folder to a page you can open
chapters.summary: The smallest reliable path from an empty folder to a Django page: a project, one app, one URL, one view and one template.
chapters.quick_answer: Run `django-admin startproject config .`, create an app with `python manage.py startapp core`, add `"core"` to `INSTALLED_APPS`, point a URL at a view, and render a template. Everything else is elaboration on those five moves.

sections.title: A project is the site; an app is a feature
sections.body:
A **project** owns settings, the root URLconf, deployment and the database connection. An **app** is a reusable bundle of models, views, templates and migrations that does one job: `accounts`, `blog`, `billing`.

You can build a whole site in one app, but keep the boundary honest. If a folder could be lifted into another project without dragging the whole site with it, it is probably an app. If it only configures this site, it belongs in the project package.

sections.title: Create it from the terminal
sections.body: Create and activate a virtual environment first, then install Django. The trailing dot in `startproject config .` is important: it puts `manage.py` in the current folder and the settings in a `config/` package, so you do not get a pointless nested folder.
sections.code:
python -m venv .venv

# Windows PowerShell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

pip install "Django>=5.2,<6.2"
django-admin startproject config .
python manage.py startapp core
python manage.py runserver
sections.note: If `django-admin` is not on PATH, use `python -m django startproject config .` instead.

sections.title: What each file is for
sections.body:
Do not memorise every file. Learn which file owns which decision.

- `manage.py` — the command entry point; always run it from the folder that contains it.
- `config/settings.py` — installed apps, database, templates, static files, security.
- `config/urls.py` — the root route table.
- `core/models.py` — database shape.
- `core/views.py` — request handling.
- `core/urls.py` — routes for this feature (create it yourself).
- `core/templates/core/` — HTML for this feature.
- `core/migrations/` — generated database history; commit it.
sections.code:
myproject/
├── manage.py
├── config/
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   ├── asgi.py
│   └── wsgi.py
├── core/
│   ├── models.py
│   ├── views.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   ├── admin.py
│   ├── migrations/
│   └── templates/core/
└── .venv/

sections.title: Wire your first page
sections.body: Three files make the request path visible. `config/urls.py` sends the root URL to the app; `core/urls.py` maps the empty path to a view; the view renders a template.
sections.code:
# config/urls.py from django.contrib import admin from django.urls import include, path urlpatterns = [ path("admin/", admin.site.urls), path("", include("core.urls")), ] # core/urls.py from django.urls import path from . import views app_name = "core" urlpatterns = [ path("", views.home, name="home"), ] # core/views.py from django.shortcuts import render def home(request): return render(request, "core/home.html", {"name": "friend"}) # core/templates/core/home.html

Hello, {{ name }}.
sections.note: Add `"core"` to `INSTALLED_APPS` before creating templates or models. Django needs the app config to discover them.

sections.title: If it does not start
sections.body:
Most first-run failures are one of these:

- `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'config'` — you are in the wrong folder, or the project package is not on `sys.path`.
- `TemplateDoesNotExist` — the app is missing from `INSTALLED_APPS`, or the template lives outside `templates/<app>/`.
- `DisallowedHost` — add the host to `ALLOWED_HOSTS`; in development `127.0.0.1` and `localhost` are enough.
- `no such table` — run `python manage.py migrate` before using auth, sessions or admin.

pitfalls: Running `manage.py` from the parent folder creates a second database and a confusing `ModuleNotFoundError`.
Creating a custom user model after the first `migrate` is painful. Decide before you migrate.
Committing `.venv/`, `db.sqlite3` or `__pycache__/` because `.gitignore` was never added.
Using the development server (`runserver`) as a production server.
checklist: Virtual environment active and Django installed.
Project package and at least one app created.
App added to `INSTALLED_APPS`.
Root URLconf includes the app URLconf.
Home page returns 200 in the browser.
`python manage.py check` passes.

chapters.title: settings.py
chapters.subtitle: The file that decides how the whole site behaves
chapters.summary: The settings that actually change behaviour, how to keep secrets out of code, and the environment-variable pattern that survives deployment.
chapters.quick_answer: Keep `SECRET_KEY` and `DEBUG` in environment variables, set `ALLOWED_HOSTS` explicitly, add every feature app to `INSTALLED_APPS`, and treat `BASE_DIR` as the anchor for every path. Local defaults are fine only while `DEBUG=True`.

sections.title: The five settings that break a new project
sections.body:
These five cause most “it worked yesterday” failures:

- `SECRET_KEY` — signing and session security. Never commit a production key.
- `DEBUG` — must be `False` in production. With `True`, Django shows tracebacks and settings.
- `ALLOWED_HOSTS` — the hostnames Django will answer for. An empty list only works in debug mode.
- `INSTALLED_APPS` — controls models, templates, admin and migrations.
- `DATABASES` — where data lives. SQLite is perfect locally and a bad default for multi-user production.

sections.title: Paths start at BASE_DIR
sections.body:
`BASE_DIR` is the folder containing `manage.py`. Build every other path from it with the `/` operator. Never concatenate strings, and never assume the current working directory.

`Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent` means: this file → its folder → the project root. If you move `settings.py`, fix this line.

sections.title: Environment variables without a library
sections.body:
A settings file should read configuration; it should not contain production secrets. Keep local defaults in code, override them from the environment, and fail loudly when a required value is missing.

Do not use `os.environ["KEY"]` for values that have a safe development default. Do use it when production cannot possibly work without the value.
sections.code:
# .env is read by your shell, Docker, or a process manager.
# Never commit the real file.
DJANGO_DEBUG=0
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=replace-with-50-random-characters
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS=example.com,www.example.com
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app

# settings.py
if not DEBUG and SECRET_KEY.startswith("dev-only"):
    raise RuntimeError("Set DJANGO_SECRET_KEY before running in production")

if not DEBUG and not ALLOWED_HOSTS:
    raise RuntimeError("Set DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS before running in production")

sections.title: Email: console in development, SMTP in production
sections.body:
Django will not send email until you configure a backend. In development, the console backend prints the message in the terminal, which is perfect for testing password-reset links. In production, use SMTP or a transactional email API.

Set `DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL` to an address your provider allows. Do not send email inside a slow request; queue it after the transaction commits. `send_mail()` is the simple path; `EmailMultiAlternatives` adds an HTML alternative.
sections.code:
# development
EMAIL_BACKEND = "django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend"
DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL = "no-reply@example.com"

# production
EMAIL_BACKEND = "django.core.mail.backends.smtp.EmailBackend"
EMAIL_HOST = "smtp.example.com"
EMAIL_PORT = 587
EMAIL_USE_TLS = True
EMAIL_HOST_USER = os.environ["EMAIL_HOST_USER"]
EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD = os.environ["EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD"]

from django.core.mail import send_mail

send_mail(
    subject="Your receipt",
    message="Thanks for your order.",
    from_email=None,  # uses DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL
    recipient_list=[user.email],
    fail_silently=False,
)
sections.note: If reset emails never arrive, check spam, the from address, SMTP credentials and whether the site URL in the email is reachable.

sections.title: Time zones, language and the admin
sections.body:
Keep `USE_TZ = True`. Store aware UTC datetimes in the database and convert only at the edge (templates, forms, reports). `TIME_ZONE` controls the default display timezone, not the stored value.

Set `LANGUAGE_CODE` for the interface language. Set `AUTH_USER_MODEL` before the first migration if you need a custom user. Set `DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD` once so every app agrees on primary-key type.
sections.code:
LANGUAGE_CODE = "en-us"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Warsaw"
USE_I18N = True
USE_TZ = True

AUTH_USER_MODEL = "accounts.User"  # only before the first migrate
DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD = "django.db.models.BigAutoField"
sections.note: Changing `AUTH_USER_MODEL` after `migrate` has run is a migration project, not a one-line edit.

sections.title: DEBUG is a security setting
sections.body:
`DEBUG=True` exposes tracebacks, SQL, settings and source snippets. Error pages are helpful locally and dangerous publicly.

Run `python manage.py check --deploy` with production settings. It flags missing `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`, insecure cookies, HSTS gaps, `DEBUG=True` and a weak secret key. Treat the output as a checklist, not a suggestion.
sections.code: python manage.py check --deploy

pitfalls: Leaving `DEBUG=True` on a public host.
Putting the production secret key in `settings.py` and committing it.
Using `ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["*"]` because the real hostname was not configured.
Changing `AUTH_USER_MODEL` after migrations already created the default user table.
Building file paths with string concatenation instead of `BASE_DIR`.
checklist: `SECRET_KEY`, `DEBUG` and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` read from the environment.
Every feature app listed in `INSTALLED_APPS`.
Templates directory and `APP_DIRS` configured.
Static and media roots set.
`USE_TZ=True` and a deliberate `TIME_ZONE`.
`check --deploy` reviewed before launch.

chapters.title: Management commands
chapters.subtitle: The terminal is part of the framework
chapters.summary: The commands worth memorising, the ones that save you in an incident, and how to add your own repeatable operation.
chapters.quick_answer: `runserver` for development, `makemigrations` + `migrate` for schema, `shell` for exploration, `test` for confidence, `collectstatic` for deployment, and `check --deploy` before launch. Put repeated operations in a custom management command, not a wiki page.

sections.title: The daily commands
sections.body:
These are the commands you will type most often. Learn what each one changes.

- `python manage.py runserver` — development server with autoreload.
- `python manage.py makemigrations` — turn model changes into migration files.
- `python manage.py migrate` — apply migrations to the database.
- `python manage.py shell` — an interactive Python shell with Django configured.
- `python manage.py test` — run the test suite.
- `python manage.py createsuperuser` — create an admin account.
- `python manage.py collectstatic` — copy static files to `STATIC_ROOT`.
sections.code:
python manage.py runserver
python manage.py makemigrations
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py shell
python manage.py test
python manage.py createsuperuser
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

sections.title: Inspect and recover
sections.body: When something is wrong, inspect before deleting. `showmigrations` tells you which files exist and which are applied. `sqlmigrate` shows the SQL a migration will run. `check` catches configuration problems without starting a server. `--plan` shows what `migrate` would do.
sections.code:
python manage.py showmigrations
python manage.py showmigrations blog
python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0002
python manage.py migrate --plan
python manage.py check
python manage.py check --deploy
python manage.py shell -c "from blog.models import Post; print(Post.objects.count())"
sections.note: `shell -c` is excellent for one-line checks in scripts and CI because it does not leave an interactive session open.

sections.title: Write a custom command
sections.body:
A management command is the right home for a repeatable operation: import a CSV, send a digest, clean expired rows. Django discovers commands in `<app>/management/commands/<name>.py`.

The class needs `help`, `add_arguments` and `handle`. Use `self.stdout.write` rather than `print`, and add `--dry-run` to anything destructive.
sections.code:
# core/management/commands/prune_drafts.py
from django.core.management.base import BaseCommand
from django.utils import timezone

from core.models import Post


class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = "Delete drafts older than the given number of days."

    def add_arguments(self, parser):
        parser.add_argument("--days", type=int, default=30)
        parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")

    def handle(self, *args, **options):
        cutoff = timezone.now() - timezone.timedelta(days=options["days"])
        queryset = Post.objects.filter(status="draft", updated_at__lt=cutoff)
        count = queryset.count()
        if options["dry_run"]:
            self.stdout.write(f"Would delete {count} drafts.")
            return
        queryset.delete()
        self.stdout.write(self.style.SUCCESS(f"Deleted {count} drafts."))
sections.note: Create `management/__init__.py` and `management/commands/__init__.py`; without them the command is invisible.

sections.title: Commands that belong in a deploy script
sections.body:
A production release usually runs these in order: install dependencies, run `migrate`, run `collectstatic`, run `check --deploy`, then restart the application server. Do not run `makemigrations` on the production host; migration files belong in version control.

Keep migrations backwards-compatible long enough for old and new application processes to overlap during a rolling deploy.
sections.code:
pip install -r requirements.txt
python manage.py migrate --noinput
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
python manage.py check --deploy
gunicorn config.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000

pitfalls: Running `makemigrations` on the production server instead of committing migration files.
Using `migrate --fake` without understanding the history; it hides drift instead of fixing it.
Writing a destructive command with no `--dry-run` and no confirmation.
Using `print()` in commands that may run under a process manager; use `self.stdout.write`.
checklist: `check` passes before every deploy.
Migrations are generated locally and committed.
`collectstatic` runs as part of release.
Destructive commands support `--dry-run`.
Custom commands live under `management/commands/` with both `__init__.py` files.

chapters.title: Django mental models
chapters.subtitle: The eight ideas that explain most Django behaviour
chapters.summary: Eight durable mental models - request pipeline, model descriptors, lazy querysets, form validation, transaction scopes, migration state, the three auth questions and async boundaries.
chapters.quick_answer: Django is a request pipeline over a lazy ORM, with explicit validation, transaction and authorization boundaries. Once those boundaries are clear, most framework behaviour stops looking magical.

sections.title: A request is a pipeline with boundaries
sections.body:
A Django request moves through a predictable path:

1. the WSGI/ASGI server creates a request
2. middleware runs from top to bottom
3. the URL resolver chooses a view
4. the view calls services, forms and the ORM
5. a response travels back through middleware

The boundaries matter more than the diagram. Session and authentication middleware populate `request.user` before the view. CSRF middleware checks unsafe methods before the view. Your view decides whether the request is authorized for this specific object.

Middleware order is behaviour: a middleware that needs `request.user` must run after `AuthenticationMiddleware`. A response middleware runs in reverse order.

A view is not the application. Put multi-step workflows in services so the same logic can be called from a command, an API or a test without constructing an HTTP request.
sections.note: Common misconception: if a URL exists, it is public. URL dispatch and authorization are separate steps.
sections.code:
# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
]

# views.py
@login_required
def invoice_detail(request, pk):
    invoice = get_object_or_404(Invoice, pk=pk, owner=request.user)
    return render(request, "invoices/detail.html", {"invoice": invoice})

sections.title: Model fields are descriptors over a database row
sections.body:
A model class is a Python class, but its fields are descriptors. `Post.title` on the class is a field object; `post.title` on an instance reads the value from the instance's state. The database row is the source of truth, and the Python object is a loaded copy.

That is why `post.save()` can write stale values, why `refresh_from_db()` exists, and why `update_fields` matters. `save()` without `update_fields` writes the fields Django considers changed; `save(update_fields=["title"])` avoids clobbering a concurrently updated column.

`Model._meta` is the metadata layer: fields, constraints, ordering, table name and relations. Use `_meta.get_field("author")` when you need field introspection, not `getattr(Post, "author")`.

A model is not a database constraint by itself. `save()` does not call `full_clean()`, and validators are not a database guarantee. Constraints belong in `Meta.constraints`; validation belongs in forms, serializers or an explicit `full_clean()` call.
sections.note: Common misconception: saving a model validates every field. It does not. Forms validate; `save()` writes.
sections.code:
post = Post.objects.get(pk=1)
post.title = "New title"
post.save(update_fields=["title"])  # do not rewrite unrelated columns

# Read back values changed by the database or another process.
post.refresh_from_db()

# Introspection uses _meta, not class attributes.
field = Post._meta.get_field("author")
print(field.remote_field.model)

sections.title: QuerySets are lazy query builders
sections.body:
A QuerySet describes SQL. It does not run until you ask for a result. That is why you can chain `.filter().exclude().order_by()` without paying for each step.

Evaluation happens when you iterate, call `list()`, index without a slice, call `len()` (which evaluates), or use `bool()`/`exists()`. `count()` runs a COUNT query, not a full fetch. Slicing with a step (`[::2]`) evaluates in Python; a simple limit slice stays lazy.

Laziness is a performance tool and a correctness trap. Reusing an evaluated QuerySet gives you cached results; modifying it returns a new QuerySet but does not clear the old cache. A QuerySet passed to a template may evaluate once, then again if you build a second one.

Build the query close to where you need it. Add `select_related`/`prefetch_related` for the shape you render, and measure with query logging before optimizing.
sections.note: Common misconception: `.filter()` executes SQL. It usually does not; evaluation does.
sections.code:
qs = Post.objects.filter(is_published=True).order_by("-created_at")
print(qs.query)          # no database hit
print(qs.exists())       # one EXISTS query
page = qs[:20]           # still lazy
posts = list(page)       # evaluates now

# Avoid evaluating just to check emptiness.
if qs.exists():
    ...

# Count in the database, not in Python.
total = qs.count()

sections.title: Forms are validation pipelines, not HTML generators
sections.body:
A form has two jobs: convert submitted data and validate it. Rendering is a third, optional job.

A form is bound when it receives data: `Form(request.POST)`. `is_valid()` runs field cleaning, form `clean()` and validators, then fills `cleaned_data`. An unbound form has no data and is never valid. `Form(request.POST or None)` is a common way to avoid binding an empty POST on GET.

`cleaned_data` is the contract your view consumes. Do not read `request.POST` after validation; use the converted values. `ModelForm.save()` writes the instance, but `commit=False` returns an unsaved object so you can set server-controlled fields.

Validation order matters: field `clean_<name>()`, then form `clean()`, then model validation if you call `full_clean()`. The database constraint is the final backstop, not the first line of defense.
sections.note: Common misconception: `is_valid()` is only for HTML forms. It is the validation boundary for any submitted data.

sections.title: Transactions are scopes, not decorators for luck
sections.body:
`transaction.atomic()` defines a scope. Everything inside commits together or rolls back together if an exception escapes. Catching an exception inside the block and continuing means the transaction is still usable, but the failed statement may have poisoned it; use a savepoint if you need to recover.

Row locks only work inside a transaction. `select_for_update()` without `atomic()` raises `TransactionManagementError`. Lock the smallest set you need, and re-check the condition after taking the lock.

`transaction.on_commit()` runs after a successful commit. It is right for cache invalidation and lightweight notifications. It is not durable: if the process dies after commit but before the callback, the callback is lost. Important side effects belong in an outbox.

Do not put a network call inside a transaction if you can avoid it. It holds locks and connections for the duration of someone else's timeout.
sections.note: Common misconception: `atomic()` makes code thread-safe. It gives all-or-nothing writes; it does not serialize every reader.

sections.title: Migrations are a state graph, not a folder of SQL
sections.body:
Migrations describe changes to Django's project state. Each migration has dependencies, operations and a state at the end. `makemigrations` compares models to that state; `migrate` applies the graph to the database.

That is why editing an applied migration is dangerous: other environments have already recorded it. Create a new migration instead. If a migration is wrong and has never left your machine, delete and regenerate it; if it reached production, write a corrective migration.

Data migrations use `RunPython` with historical models from `apps.get_model()`. Do not import current models into a data migration: the schema at that point may not match today's code. Keep schema changes and large backfills in separate migrations.

`sqlmigrate` shows the SQL for one migration. `migrate --plan` shows what will run. Both are cheap checks before a production deploy.
sections.note: Common misconception: migrations are just generated SQL. They are state transitions that Django uses to build the next state.
sections.code:
python manage.py makemigrations
python manage.py sqlmigrate shop 0042
python manage.py migrate --plan
python manage.py migrate

# Data migration skeleton
python manage.py makemigrations shop --empty -n backfill_status

sections.title: Authentication, authorization and CSRF are three questions
sections.body:
Keep three questions separate:

- Authentication: who is making the request? `request.user`, session or token.
- Authorization: may this user perform this action on this object? Permissions, ownership, roles.
- CSRF: did this state-changing request come from a page we served? A token, not a login check.

A login guard answers only the first question. It does not stop user A from editing user B's invoice. Filter the queryset by the current user or an explicit membership relation, and return 404 when the object should not be visible.

CSRF protects cookie-authenticated unsafe methods. It is not relevant to a pure token API that does not use cookies, but it is critical for a browser session. Do not disable it globally to fix one endpoint.

Superuser is not a substitute for object permissions. Test anonymous, owner, other-user and staff paths separately.
sections.note: Common misconception: `login_required` means the object is safe. It only proves someone is logged in.

sections.title: Async changes concurrency, not the ORM
sections.body:
An async view lets the server handle other requests while this one awaits I/O. It does not make CPU work faster, and it does not make the synchronous Django ORM async.

Inside an async view, use `await sync_to_async(...)` for blocking ORM calls, or keep the view synchronous and let the worker handle concurrency. Do not call the sync ORM directly from async code; Django will raise `SynchronousOnlyOperation`.

Long tasks - email, PDF generation, video processing, third-party calls with retries - belong in a worker, not in the request/response cycle. A background job also gives you retries and a place to observe failure.

Choose async when you have many concurrent I/O-bound requests and an ASGI deployment. Choose a worker when the work is long or must survive a restart. They solve different problems.
sections.note: Common misconception: `async def` makes a slow database query fast. It only changes how the process waits.
sections.code:
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async

async def dashboard(request):
    # The ORM is synchronous; run it off the event loop.
    invoices = await sync_to_async(list)(
        Invoice.objects.filter(owner=request.user)[:20]
    )
    return render(request, "dashboard.html", {"invoices": invoices})

# Long work belongs in a task queue, not in this view.
# send_invoice_email.delay(invoice.pk)

pitfalls: Treating a URL as authorization.
Assuming `save()` validates all fields.
Evaluating a QuerySet repeatedly in a template or loop.
Putting network calls inside a transaction.
Editing a migration that already reached production.
Using `login_required` as the only object-level check.
Marking a view `async` and calling the sync ORM directly.
checklist: I can trace a request through middleware, URL, view and response.
I know when a QuerySet evaluates.
Forms are the validation boundary; constraints are the backstop.
Transactions own all-or-nothing writes and row locks.
Migrations are state transitions, not editable SQL files.
Authentication, authorization and CSRF are separate checks.
Async is for I/O concurrency; workers are for long tasks.
